analysis.investment_thesis: Asahi India Glass is a capable industrial company in a capital-intensive, commodity-adjacent business, but its 8.5% revenue CAGR over nine years and structurally thin FCF make it antithetical to Fisher's growth framework. At a P/E of 69x and EV/EBITDA of 32x, investors are paying growth-company prices for a slow-growth business with rapidly rising debt.
key_strengths: Dominant market position in Indian automotive glass (OEM supply to virtually every car maker) creates sticky, long-term customer relationships consistent with Fisher's 'worthwhile profit margin' criterion
Gross margin of 64.97% reflects genuine pricing power and product quality differentiation in laminated/tempered auto glass
Revenue has recovered strongly post-COVID — 8.5% CAGR over 9 years, with the 2022-2025 period accelerating as auto production normalised
key_risks: Revenue CAGR of 8.5% is far below Fisher's 20-30% growth threshold; at this growth rate the 69x P/E implies a decade-plus of perfect execution with no margin compression
Free cash flow turned deeply negative in FY24 (₹-244 Cr) and FY25 (₹-536 Cr) as capex ramped to ₹1,268 Cr — the business is consuming cash, not generating it
Borrowings surged from ₹1,401 Cr (FY23) to ₹2,856 Cr (FY25), pushing D/E to 0.77 — leverage is rising materially as cash generation remains weak
red_flags: EBITDA has been essentially flat from ₹817 Cr (FY23) to ₹782 Cr (FY25) while the company took on ₹1,455 Cr of incremental debt — returns on the expansion are not yet visible
ROE of 13.6% and ROCE of 12.4% are mediocre and declining — the heavy capex cycle has not improved capital productivity
At P/E 69x with 8.5% revenue growth, the stock prices in growth that the company has never historically delivered
analysis.detailed_analysis: From a Fisher lens, Asahi India Glass fails the fundamental test: is this a company with products offering sufficient market potential for sustained, above-average sales growth? The nine-year revenue CAGR of 8.5% says no. Glass manufacturing is capital-intensive, cyclical, and subject to commoditisation — not fertile ground for the innovation-driven moats Fisher prizes. The automotive glass segment benefits from OEM relationships, but auto glass is ultimately a specifications-driven commodity differentiated by quality and reliability, not proprietary technology. The current capex super-cycle (₹2,169 Cr over FY24-FY25) is consuming the balance sheet without visible margin improvement — EBITDA is flat while debt is up ~100% in two years. The valuation at 69x trailing P/E for a slow-growth, capital-heavy business with negative FCF is deeply puzzling. Fisher would note that the market appears to be pricing in a float glass and architectural glass boom that has yet to materialise. Until FCF turns positive, debt stabilises, and ROE climbs sustainably above 15%, this is a business to watch rather than own.
